\section*{Simultaneous Equations 01\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-001)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 01 (ise2-001)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 5x + 2y = 16 \) and \( 3x - 2y = 0 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations and notice the \( y \)-coefficients already match in magnitude.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 5x + 2y = 16 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 3x - 2y = 0
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients are \( +2 \) and \( -2 \), so adding eliminates \( y \) immediately.

\textit{Step 2: Add equations \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{2} \) to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(5x + 2y) + (3x - 2y) = 16 + 0 \implies 8x = 16 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel out.

\textit{Step 3: Substitute \( x = 2 \) into equation \( \textcircled{2} \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(2) - 2y = 0 \implies 6 = 2y \implies y = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Choose the simpler equation to substitute back into.

\textit{Step 4: Check in equation \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5(2) + 2(3) = 10 + 6 = 16 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both values satisfy the first equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 2,\; y = 3 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 02\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-002)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 02 (ise2-002)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 4x + y = 14 \) and \( 2x - 3y = -8 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 4x + y = 14 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 2x - 3y = -8
\end{gathered}\]
Equation \( \textcircled{1} \) has \( y \) with coefficient \( +1 \), so multiplying \( \textcircled{1} \) by 3 will make the \( y \)-coefficients \( +3 \) and \( -3 \). Adding then eliminates \( y \) cleanly.

\textit{Step 2: Multiply equation \( \textcircled{1} \) by 3.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 12x + 3y = 42
\end{gathered}\]
Multiplying every term by the same non-zero constant preserves the solution set --- the new equation has identical solutions to the original.

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{3} \) and \( \textcircled{2} \) to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(12x + 3y) + (2x - 3y) = 42 + (-8) \implies 14x = 34 \implies x = \tfrac{17}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel because their coefficients are opposite. A non-integer solution is perfectly valid --- not every linear system has whole-number answers.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = \tfrac{17}{7} \) into equation \( \textcircled{1} \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 14 - 4 \times \tfrac{17}{7} = \tfrac{98}{7} - \tfrac{68}{7} = \tfrac{30}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
Back-substitute into the simpler equation. Use a common denominator: \( 14 = \tfrac{98}{7} \), then subtract numerators.

\textit{Step 5: Check in equation \( \textcircled{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times \tfrac{17}{7} - 3 \times \tfrac{30}{7} = \tfrac{34 - 90}{7} = \tfrac{-56}{7} = -8 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Always verify by substituting into the OTHER equation (not the one used for back-substitution) --- this catches arithmetic slips.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{17}{7},\; y = \dfrac{30}{7} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 03\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-003)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 03 (ise2-003)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 3x + 4y = 10 \) and \( 5x - 2y = 8 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 3x + 4y = 10 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 5x - 2y = 8
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 2 to match the \( y \)-coefficient.

\textit{Step 2: Multiply equation \( \textcircled{2} \) by 2.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 10x - 4y = 16
\end{gathered}\]
Now \( y \)-coefficients are \( +4 \) and \( -4 \).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{3} \) to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(3x + 4y) + (10x - 4y) = 10 + 16 \implies 13x = 26 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = 2 \) into \( \textcircled{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5(2) - 2y = 8 \implies 10 - 2y = 8 \implies y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Solve for \( y \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(2) + 4(1) = 6 + 4 = 10 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
The solution satisfies the first equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 2,\; y = 1 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 04\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-004)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 04 (ise2-004)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 7x - 3y = 11 \) and \( 4x + 5y = 33 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 7x - 3y = 11 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 4x + 5y = 33
\end{gathered}\]
Neither pair of coefficients matches, so we scale both equations to align the \( y \)-coefficients. Multiply \( \textcircled{1} \) by 5 and \( \textcircled{2} \) by 3 so the \( y \)-coefficients become \( -15 \) and \( +15 \).

\textit{Step 2: Scale both equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 35x - 15y = 55 \qquad \textcircled{4}\; 12x + 15y = 99
\end{gathered}\]
Scaling preserves the solution set of each equation. The \( y \)-coefficients are now opposite in sign, so adding will eliminate \( y \).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{3} \) and \( \textcircled{4} \) to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(35x - 15y) + (12x + 15y) = 55 + 99 \implies 47x = 154 \implies x = \tfrac{154}{47}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel. The fact that the answer is fractional is not an error --- these particular coefficients simply do not produce integer solutions.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = \tfrac{154}{47} \) into \( \textcircled{1} \) and solve for \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
7 \times \tfrac{154}{47} - 3y = 11 \implies \tfrac{1078}{47} - 3y = \tfrac{517}{47} \implies 3y = \tfrac{561}{47} \implies y = \tfrac{187}{47}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert 11 to a fraction with denominator 47 (\( 11 = \tfrac{517}{47} \)) before subtracting, then divide by 3. Sign track carefully when moving the \( 3y \) term across.

\textit{Step 5: Check in equation \( \textcircled{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 \times \tfrac{154}{47} + 5 \times \tfrac{187}{47} = \tfrac{616 + 935}{47} = \tfrac{1551}{47} = 33 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute both values into the equation NOT used for back-substitution to confirm correctness.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{154}{47},\; y = \dfrac{187}{47} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 05\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-005)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 05 (ise2-005)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 2x + 5y = 19 \) and \( 6x - y = 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 2x + 5y = 19 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 6x - y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 5 to match the \( y \)-coefficient.

\textit{Step 2: Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 5.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 30x - 5y = 5
\end{gathered}\]
\( y \)-coefficients are now \( +5 \) and \( -5 \).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{3} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x + 5y) + (30x - 5y) = 19 + 5 \implies 32x = 24 \implies x = \tfrac{3}{4}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = \tfrac{3}{4} \) into \( \textcircled{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
6 \times \tfrac{3}{4} - y = 1 \implies \tfrac{9}{2} - y = 1 \implies y = \tfrac{7}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Solve for \( y \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times \tfrac{3}{4} + 5 \times \tfrac{7}{2} = \tfrac{3}{2} + \tfrac{35}{2} = \tfrac{38}{2} = 19 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{3}{4},\; y = \dfrac{7}{2} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 06\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-006)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 06 (ise2-006)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 5x + 3y = 7 \) and \( 2x - y = -8 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 5x + 3y = 7 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 2x - y = -8
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients are \( +3 \) and \( -1 \). Multiplying \( \textcircled{2} \) by 3 makes them \( +3 \) and \( -3 \), so adding will eliminate \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 3.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 6x - 3y = -24
\end{gathered}\]
Multiplying every term by 3 keeps \( \textcircled{2} \) true (linear combinations preserve solutions).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{3} \) to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(5x + 3y) + (6x - 3y) = 7 + (-24) \implies 11x = -17 \implies x = -\tfrac{17}{11}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel because their coefficients sum to zero. Negative and fractional values are valid solutions --- keep going.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = -\tfrac{17}{11} \) into \( \textcircled{2} \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times \left(-\tfrac{17}{11}\right) - y = -8 \implies -\tfrac{34}{11} - y = -\tfrac{88}{11} \implies y = \tfrac{54}{11}
\end{gathered}\]
Equation \( \textcircled{2} \) is simpler (\( y \) has coefficient \( -1 \)). Rewrite \( -8 \) as \( -\tfrac{88}{11} \) so both sides share a denominator.

\textit{Step 5: Check in equation \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5 \times \left(-\tfrac{17}{11}\right) + 3 \times \tfrac{54}{11} = \tfrac{-85 + 162}{11} = \tfrac{77}{11} = 7 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Substituting into the OTHER equation confirms both values are correct.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = -\dfrac{17}{11},\; y = \dfrac{54}{11} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 07\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-007)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 07 (ise2-007)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 3x + 2y = 12 \) and \( x - 4y = -4 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 3x + 2y = 12 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; x - 4y = -4
\end{gathered}\]
Equation \( \textcircled{2} \) has \( x \) with coefficient \( +1 \), so substitution is clean: rearrange \( \textcircled{2} \) for \( x \) and substitute into \( \textcircled{1} \).

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange \( \textcircled{2} \) to express \( x \) in terms of \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 4y - 4
\end{gathered}\]
Add \( 4y \) to both sides. Keeping \( x \) isolated lets us substitute it cleanly into the other equation.

\textit{Step 3: Substitute into \( \textcircled{1} \) and solve for \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(4y - 4) + 2y = 12 \implies 12y - 12 + 2y = 12 \implies 14y = 24 \implies y = \tfrac{12}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
Distribute the \( 3 \) carefully across both terms inside the bracket, then collect like terms. A fractional answer is perfectly valid.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( y = \tfrac{12}{7} \) back into the rearranged equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 4 \times \tfrac{12}{7} - 4 = \tfrac{48}{7} - \tfrac{28}{7} = \tfrac{20}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
Use a common denominator when subtracting (\( 4 = \tfrac{28}{7} \)).

\textit{Step 5: Check in equation \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 \times \tfrac{20}{7} + 2 \times \tfrac{12}{7} = \tfrac{60 + 24}{7} = \tfrac{84}{7} = 12 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Always verify by substituting into the OTHER equation --- the one not used to express \( x \) in terms of \( y \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{20}{7},\; y = \dfrac{12}{7} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 08\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-008)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 08 (ise2-008)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 4x - 3y = -1 \) and \( 3x + y = 9 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Label the equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 4x - 3y = -1 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 3x + y = 9
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 3 to match the \( y \)-coefficient in \( \textcircled{1} \).

\textit{Step 2: Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 3.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 9x + 3y = 27
\end{gathered}\]
\( y \)-coefficients: \( -3 \) and \( +3 \).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{3} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
13x = 26 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel.

\textit{Step 4: Substitute \( x = 2 \) into \( \textcircled{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(2) + y = 9 \implies y = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Solve for \( y \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4(2) - 3(3) = 8 - 9 = -1 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Solution verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 2,\; y = 3 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 09\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-009)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 09 (ise2-009)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find the point of intersection of the lines \( y = 3x - 1 \) and \( y = -x + 7 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the right-hand sides equal (since both equal \( y \)).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3x - 1 = -x + 7
\end{gathered}\]
At the intersection point the \( y \)-values are equal.

\textit{Step 2: Solve for \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4x = 8 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Collect \( x \) terms on the left and constants on the right.

\textit{Step 3: Find \( y \) using the first equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3(2) - 1 = 5
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 2 \).

\textit{Step 4: Check in the second equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = -2 + 7 = 5 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both equations give \( y = 5 \) at \( x = 2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Point of intersection:  (2, 5) 
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 10\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-010)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 10 (ise2-010)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find the point of intersection of the lines \( y = -2x + 10 \) and \( y = 4x - 2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the expressions for \( y \) equal.}
\[\begin{gathered}
-2x + 10 = 4x - 2
\end{gathered}\]
Both expressions equal \( y \) at the intersection.

\textit{Step 2: Solve for \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
12 = 6x \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Add \( 2x \) and add 2 to both sides.

\textit{Step 3: Find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 4(2) - 2 = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Use the second equation.

\textit{Step 4: Check in the first equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = -2(2) + 10 = 6 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Point of intersection:  (2, 6) 
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 11\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-011)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 11 (ise2-011)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 3x - 4y + 1 = 0 \) and \( 5x + 2y - 11 = 0 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange both equations into standard form.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{1}\; 3x - 4y = -1 \qquad \textcircled{2}\; 5x + 2y = 11
\end{gathered}\]
Move the constant to the right-hand side in each.

\textit{Step 2: Multiply \( \textcircled{2} \) by 2 to match \( y \)-coefficients.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\textcircled{3}\; 10x + 4y = 22
\end{gathered}\]
\( y \)-coefficients: \( -4 \) and \( +4 \).

\textit{Step 3: Add \( \textcircled{1} \) and \( \textcircled{3} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
13x = 21 \implies x = \tfrac{21}{13}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) terms cancel.

\textit{Step 4: Use \( \textcircled{2} \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5 \times \tfrac{21}{13} + 2y = 11 \implies 2y = 11 - \tfrac{105}{13} = \tfrac{143-105}{13} = \tfrac{38}{13} \implies y = \tfrac{19}{13}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute and solve for \( y \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( \textcircled{1} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 \times \tfrac{21}{13} - 4 \times \tfrac{19}{13} = \tfrac{63 - 76}{13} = \tfrac{-13}{13} = -1 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Solution verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{21}{13},\; y = \dfrac{19}{13} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 12\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-012)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 12 (ise2-012)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 7}

\question{Three paths in a park are modelled by the equations \( A: 2x + y = 8 \), \( B: x - y = 1 \), \( C: x + 3y = 12 \). Benches are placed at each intersection. Find the coordinates of all benches.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Find intersection of \( A \) and \( B \): \( 2x + y = 8 \) and \( x - y = 1 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{Add: } 3x = 9 \implies x = 3,\quad y = 3 - 1 = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Adding eliminates \( y \) directly.

\textit{Step 2: Find intersection of \( A \) and \( C \): \( 2x + y = 8 \) and \( x + 3y = 12 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\times 3: 6x + 3y = 24; \quad \text{subtract }C: 5x = 12 \implies x = \tfrac{12}{5},\quad y = 8 - 2 \times \tfrac{12}{5} = \tfrac{16}{5}
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( A \) by 3 and subtract \( C \).

\textit{Step 3: Find intersection of \( B \) and \( C \): \( x - y = 1 \) and \( x + 3y = 12 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{Subtract }B\text{ from }C: 4y = 11 \implies y = \tfrac{11}{4},\quad x = 1 + \tfrac{11}{4} = \tfrac{15}{4}
\end{gathered}\]
Subtracting eliminates \( x \).

\textit{Step 4: State all three bench coordinates.}
\[\begin{gathered}
A \cap B = (3, 2),\quad A \cap C = \left(\tfrac{12}{5}, \tfrac{16}{5}\right),\quad B \cap C = \left(\tfrac{15}{4}, \tfrac{11}{4}\right)
\end{gathered}\]
Three distinct intersection points.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Benches at  (3, 2) ,  ($\tfrac{12}{5}$, $\tfrac{16}{5}$) , and  ($\tfrac{15}{4}$, $\tfrac{11}{4}$) .
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 13\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-013)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 13 (ise2-013)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = x + 3 \) and \( y = x^2 - 3 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: The linear equation already expresses \( y \) in terms of \( x \). Substitute into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x + 3 = x^2 - 3
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) in the quadratic equation with \( x + 3 \).

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange to form a quadratic equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - x - 6 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side: \( x^2 - x - 3 - 3 = 0 \).

\textit{Step 3: Factorise the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 3)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = 3 \text{ or } x = -2
\end{gathered}\]
We need two numbers that multiply to \(-6\) and add to \(-1\): these are \(-3\) and \(2\).

\textit{Step 4: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values using \( y = x + 3 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 3 \Rightarrow y = 6; \quad x = -2 \Rightarrow y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into the linear equation.

\textit{Step 5: Check both pairs in the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x=3: 9-3=6\checkmark \quad x=-2: 4-3=1\checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both solutions verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 3,\; y = 6  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = -2,\; y = 1 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 14\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-014)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 14 (ise2-014)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = 2x - 1 \) and \( y = x^2 - 2x + 3 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Substitute \( y = 2x - 1 \) into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x - 1 = x^2 - 2x + 3
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) in the second equation.

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - 4x + 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 2)^2 = 0 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
A perfect square --- the line is tangent to the curve, so there is exactly one solution.

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2(2) - 1 = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 2 \) into the linear equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad  x = 2,  y = 3  (the line is tangent to the curve at this point)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 15\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-015)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 15 (ise2-015)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( x + y = 5 \) and \( x^2 + y^2 = 17 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 5 - x
\end{gathered}\]
Express \( y \) in terms of \( x \) from the linear equation.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the quadratic equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + (5 - x)^2 = 17 \implies x^2 + 25 - 10x + x^2 = 17 \implies 2x^2 - 10x + 8 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand \( (5-x)^2 \) and collect terms.

\textit{Step 3: Divide through by 2 and factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0 \implies (x-1)(x-4) = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 4 and adding to \(-5\): \(-1\) and \(-4\).

\textit{Step 4: Find the \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 4; \quad x = 4 \Rightarrow y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into \( y = 5 - x \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( x^2 + y^2 = 17 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
1 + 16 = 17 \checkmark \quad \text{and} \quad 16 + 1 = 17 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both pairs satisfy the circle equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 1,\; y = 4  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = 4,\; y = 1 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 16\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-016)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 16 (ise2-016)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = 3x - 5 \) and \( x^2 + y^2 = 25 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Substitute \( y = 3x - 5 \) into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + (3x-5)^2 = 25
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) in the second equation.

\textit{Step 2: Expand and simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 9x^2 - 30x + 25 = 25 \implies 10x^2 - 30x = 0 \implies 10x(x - 3) = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand, then collect terms and factorise.

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 0 \text{ or } x = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Two solutions from the factorisation.

\textit{Step 4: Find the \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x=0 \Rightarrow y = -5; \quad x=3 \Rightarrow y = 4
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute into \( y = 3x - 5 \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( x^2 + y^2 = 25 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
0 + 25 = 25 \checkmark \quad 9 + 16 = 25 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both solutions verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 0,\; y = -5  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = 3,\; y = 4 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 17\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-017)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 17 (ise2-017)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 2x - y = 1 \) and \( x^2 + y^2 = 10 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2x - 1
\end{gathered}\]
Isolate \( y \) in the linear equation.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + (2x-1)^2 = 10 \implies x^2 + 4x^2 - 4x + 1 = 10 \implies 5x^2 - 4x - 9 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and collect terms.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(5x - 9)(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = \tfrac{9}{5} \text{ or } x = -1
\end{gathered}\]
Check: \( 5 \times (-9) = -45 \) and \( -9 + 5 = -4 \). \( \checkmark \)

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \tfrac{9}{5} \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{13}{5}; \quad x = -1 \Rightarrow y = -3
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( y = 2x - 1 \).

\textit{Step 5: Check \( x = -1, y = -3 \) in the circle.}
\[\begin{gathered}
1 + 9 = 10 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Solution verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{9}{5},\; y = \dfrac{13}{5}  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = -1,\; y = -3 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 18\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-018)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 18 (ise2-018)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Find the points of intersection of the curve \( y = x^2 + 3x - 4 \) and the line \( y = 2x + 2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the expressions for \( y \) equal.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 3x - 4 = 2x + 2
\end{gathered}\]
At an intersection point both equations give the same \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + x - 6 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x + 3)(x - 2) = 0 \implies x = -3 \text{ or } x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to \(-6\) and adding to \(1\).

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \)-values using \( y = 2x + 2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = -3 \Rightarrow y = -4; \quad x = 2 \Rightarrow y = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into the linear equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Points of intersection:  (-3, -4)  and  (2, 6) 
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 19\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-019)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 19 (ise2-019)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Find the points of intersection of \( x^2 + y^2 = 45 \) and \( x + 2y = 0 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = -2y
\end{gathered}\]
Express \( x \) in terms of \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(-2y)^2 + y^2 = 45 \implies 4y^2 + y^2 = 45 \implies 5y^2 = 45 \implies y^2 = 9
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and simplify.

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3 \text{ or } y = -3
\end{gathered}\]
Take both square roots.

\textit{Step 4: Find corresponding \( x \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3 \Rightarrow x = -6; \quad y = -3 \Rightarrow x = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( x = -2y \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in the circle.}
\[\begin{gathered}
36 + 9 = 45 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both pairs satisfy the circle equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  (-6,\ 3)  \) and \(\displaystyle   (6,\ -3) \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 20\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-020)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 20 (ise2-020)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = x^2 - 5x + 4 \) and \( y = x - 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Substitute \( y = x - 1 \) into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x - 1 = x^2 - 5x + 4
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) in the first equation.

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 1)(x - 5) = 0 \implies x = 1 \text{ or } x = 5
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 5 and adding to \(-6\): \(-1\) and \(-5\).

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \)-values using \( y = x - 1 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 0; \quad x = 5 \Rightarrow y = 4
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute into the linear equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 1,\; y = 0  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = 5,\; y = 4 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 21\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-021)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 21 (ise2-021)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( xy = 8 \) and \( y - x = 2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Express \( y \) in terms of \( x \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into \( xy = 8 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x(x + 2) = 8 \implies x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and rearrange.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0 \implies x = -4 \text{ or } x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to \(-8\) and adding to \(2\): \(4\) and \(-2\).

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = -4 \Rightarrow y = -2; \quad x = 2 \Rightarrow y = 4
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( y = x + 2 \).

\textit{Step 5: Check in \( xy = 8 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(-4)(-2) = 8 \checkmark \quad 2 \times 4 = 8 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Both solutions verified.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = -4,\; y = -2  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = 2,\; y = 4 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 22\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-022)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 22 (ise2-022)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = 2x^2 - x - 3 \) and \( y = 3x - 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Substitute \( y = 3x - 1 \) into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
3x - 1 = 2x^2 - x - 3
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) in the first equation.

\textit{Step 2: Rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x^2 - 4x - 2 = 0 \implies x^2 - 2x - 1 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Divide through by 2.

\textit{Step 3: Use the quadratic formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( a=1, b=-2, c=-1 \implies \Delta = 4 + 4 = 8 \).

\textit{Step 4: Find the \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3(1 \pm \sqrt{2}) - 1 = 2 \pm 3\sqrt{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( y = 3x - 1 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = 1 + \sqrt{2},\; y = 2 + 3\sqrt{2}  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = 1 - \sqrt{2},\; y = 2 - 3\sqrt{2} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 23\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-023)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 23 (ise2-023)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Find the points of intersection of the line \( 3x - y + 2 = 0 \) and the curve \( y = x^2 + 2x - 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation for \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3x + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Add \( y \) to both sides and subtract \( 3x \) and \( 2 \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the curve equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
3x + 2 = x^2 + 2x - 1 \implies x^2 - x - 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange to standard quadratic form.

\textit{Step 3: Apply the quadratic formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 12}}{2} = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = 1 + 12 = 13 \); does not factorise over the integers.

\textit{Step 4: Find the \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3 \times \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2} + 2 = \frac{7 \pm 3\sqrt{13}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute into \( y = 3x + 2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{13}}{2},\ \dfrac{7+3\sqrt{13}}{2}\right)  \) and \(\displaystyle   \left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{13}}{2},\ \dfrac{7-3\sqrt{13}}{2}\right) \)
\end{answerbox}
\textbf{Diagram.}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 24\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-024)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 24 (ise2-024)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 7}

\question{a) Solve the simultaneous equations \( x^2 + y^2 = 20 \) and \( y = 2x - 10 \). \\[3pt] b) State what your answer tells you geometrically about the line and the circle.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Substitute \( y = 2x - 10 \) into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + (2x-10)^2 = 20 \implies x^2 + 4x^2 - 40x + 100 = 20
\end{gathered}\]
Expand \( (2x-10)^2 = 4x^2 - 40x + 100 \).

\textit{Step 2: Simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
5x^2 - 40x + 80 = 0 \implies x^2 - 8x + 16 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Divide through by 5.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 4)^2 = 0 \implies x = 4
\end{gathered}\]
Perfect square --- only one solution.

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2(4) - 10 = -2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 4 \) into the linear equation.

\textit{Step 5: Part b: interpret geometrically.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{One solution } \Rightarrow \text{ the line is tangent to the circle at } (4, -2)
\end{gathered}\]
A repeated root from the quadratic means the line touches the circle at exactly one point.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad a)  x = 4,  y = -2    b) The line is tangent to the circle at the point  (4, -2) .
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 25\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-025)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 25 (ise2-025)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Without solving fully, determine whether the line \( y = 2x + 5 \) and the curve \( y = x^2 - x + 2 \) intersect at zero, one, or two points.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the equations equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x + 5 = x^2 - x + 2 \implies x^2 - 3x - 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 2: Compute the discriminant \( \Delta = b^2 - 4ac \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = (-3)^2 - 4(1)(-3) = 9 + 12 = 21
\end{gathered}\]
Here \( a=1, b=-3, c=-3 \).

\textit{Step 3: Interpret the discriminant.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = 21 > 0 \implies \text{two distinct real intersections}
\end{gathered}\]
A positive discriminant means two distinct real roots, hence two points of intersection.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad The line and curve intersect at \textbf{two} points (since  $\Delta$ = 21 $>$ 0 ).
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 26\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-026)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 26 (ise2-026)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Without solving fully, determine whether the line \( y = 4x - 5 \) and the curve \( y = x^2 + 2x + 3 \) intersect, and if so how many times.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
4x - 5 = x^2 + 2x + 3 \implies x^2 - 2x + 8 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 2: Compute the discriminant.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(8) = 4 - 32 = -28
\end{gathered}\]
\( a=1, b=-2, c=8 \).

\textit{Step 3: Interpret.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = -28 < 0 \implies \text{no real intersections}
\end{gathered}\]
A negative discriminant means no real roots --- the line does not meet the curve.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad The line and curve do \textbf{not intersect} (since  $\Delta$ = -28 $<$ 0 ).
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 27\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-027)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 27 (ise2-027)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Without solving fully, determine whether the line \( y = 6x - 9 \) and the curve \( y = x^2 + 3 \) intersect at zero, one, or two points, and state the geometric significance.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
6x - 9 = x^2 + 3 \implies x^2 - 6x + 12 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 2: Compute the discriminant.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = 36 - 48 = -12
\end{gathered}\]
\( a=1, b=-6, c=12 \).

\textit{Step 3: Interpret.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = -12 < 0 \implies \text{no real intersections}
\end{gathered}\]
The line does not touch or cross the curve at any real point.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad No intersections ( $\Delta$ $<$ 0 ): the line misses the curve entirely.
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 28\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-028)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 28 (ise2-028)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Without solving fully, determine whether the line \( y = 5x - 4 \) and the curve \( y = x^2 + 2x + 1 \) intersect at zero, one, or two points.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
5x - 4 = x^2 + 2x + 1 \implies x^2 - 3x + 5 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Bring all terms to one side.

\textit{Step 2: Compute the discriminant.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = 9 - 20 = -11
\end{gathered}\]
\( a=1, b=-3, c=5 \).

\textit{Step 3: Interpret.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = -11 < 0 \implies \text{no real intersections}
\end{gathered}\]
The line and curve do not meet.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad No intersections ( $\Delta$ = -11 $<$ 0 ).
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 29\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-029)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 29 (ise2-029)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 6}

\question{A straight line has equation \( y = kx + 2 \). Find the values of \( k \) for which the line is tangent to the curve \( y = x^2 - 4x + 6 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the expressions for \( y \) equal.}
\[\begin{gathered}
kx + 2 = x^2 - 4x + 6 \implies x^2 - (4+k)x + 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange to a quadratic in \( x \).

\textit{Step 2: For tangency, the discriminant must equal zero.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = (4+k)^2 - 16 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
A tangent line meets the curve at exactly one point \( \Leftrightarrow \Delta = 0 \).

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( k \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(4+k)^2 = 16 \implies 4 + k = \pm 4
\end{gathered}\]
Take square roots of both sides.

\textit{Step 4: Find both values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
k = 0 \text{ or } k = -8
\end{gathered}\]
\( 4 + k = 4 \Rightarrow k = 0 \);   \( 4 + k = -4 \Rightarrow k = -8 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  k = 0  \) or \(\displaystyle   k = -8 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 30\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-030)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 30 (ise2-030)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Two positive numbers \( x \) and \( y \) satisfy \( x + y = 10 \) and \( xy = 24 \). Find the two numbers.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the linear equation, express \( y \) in terms of \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 10 - x
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange the first equation.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into \( xy = 24 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x(10 - x) = 24 \implies 10x - x^2 = 24 \implies x^2 - 10x + 24 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and rearrange.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 4)(x - 6) = 0 \implies x = 4 \text{ or } x = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 24 and adding to \(-10\): \(-4\) and \(-6\).

\textit{Step 4: Find corresponding \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 4 \Rightarrow y = 6; \quad x = 6 \Rightarrow y = 4
\end{gathered}\]
The two numbers are 4 and 6 (the same pair, just swapped).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad The two numbers are  4  and  6 .
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 31\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-031)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 31 (ise2-031)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( 3x + y = 7 \) and \( x^2 - y = 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the linear equation, isolate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 7 - 3x
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange equation \( \textcircled{1} \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the quadratic equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - (7 - 3x) = 1 \implies x^2 + 3x - 8 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( y \) and simplify.

\textit{Step 3: Use the quadratic formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 32}}{2} = \frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{41}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = 9 + 32 = 41 \); cannot factorise over the integers.

\textit{Step 4: Find \( y \) for each solution.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 7 - 3 \times \frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{41}}{2} = \frac{14 + 9 \mp 3\sqrt{41}}{2} = \frac{23 \mp 3\sqrt{41}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \) into \( y = 7 - 3x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x = \dfrac{-3+\sqrt{41}}{2},\; y = \dfrac{23-3\sqrt{41}}{2}  \) and \(\displaystyle   x = \dfrac{-3-\sqrt{41}}{2},\; y = \dfrac{23+3\sqrt{41}}{2} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 32\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-032)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 32 (ise2-032)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 6}

\question{A rectangle has perimeter 26 cm and area 42 cm\textsuperscript{2}. \\[3pt] a) Let the length be \( x \) cm and width \( y \) cm. Write down two equations in \( x \) and \( y \). \\[3pt] b) Hence find the dimensions of the rectangle.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Part a: write equations from perimeter and area.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x + 2y = 26 \implies x + y = 13 \qquad xy = 42
\end{gathered}\]
Perimeter \( = 2(x+y) \); area \( = xy \).

\textit{Step 2: Part b: from the linear equation, express \( y \) in terms of \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 13 - x
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange the perimeter equation.

\textit{Step 3: Substitute into the area equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x(13 - x) = 42 \implies x^2 - 13x + 42 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and rearrange.

\textit{Step 4: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 6)(x - 7) = 0 \implies x = 6 \text{ or } x = 7
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 42 and adding to \(-13\): \(-6\) and \(-7\).

\textit{Step 5: State the dimensions.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 7,\ y = 6 \quad \text{(or equivalently } x=6, y=7\text{)}
\end{gathered}\]
Both give the same rectangle: 7 cm by 6 cm.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad a)  x + y = 13  and  xy = 42    b) Dimensions:  7  cm by  6  cm.
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 33\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-033)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 33 (ise2-033)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 6}

\question{Solve the simultaneous equations \( x^2 + y^2 = 34 \) and \( x - y = -2 \), and state the geometric meaning of your answer.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = y - 2
\end{gathered}\]
Express \( x \) in terms of \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(y-2)^2 + y^2 = 34 \implies y^2 - 4y + 4 + y^2 = 34 \implies 2y^2 - 4y - 30 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and collect terms.

\textit{Step 3: Divide by 2 and factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y^2 - 2y - 15 = 0 \implies (y - 5)(y + 3) = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to \(-15\) and adding to \(-2\): \(-5\) and \(3\).

\textit{Step 4: Find \( x \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 5 \Rightarrow x = 3; \quad y = -3 \Rightarrow x = -5
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( x = y - 2 \).

\textit{Step 5: State the geometric meaning.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{Two intersection points } (3, 5) \text{ and } (-5, -3)
\end{gathered}\]
The line \( x - y = -2 \) is a chord of the circle \( x^2 + y^2 = 34 \), crossing it at two points.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad  (3, 5)  and  (-5, -3) . The line is a chord of the circle  $x^2$ + $y^2$ = 34 .
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 34\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-034)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 34 (ise2-034)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 8}

\question{a) Solve the simultaneous equations \( y = x^2 + 2x - 8 \) and \( y + 3x = 4 \). \\[3pt] b) Interpret your answer geometrically. \\[3pt] c) Find the length of the chord joining the two points of intersection.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Part a: rearrange the linear equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 4 - 3x
\end{gathered}\]
Isolate \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 - 3x = x^2 + 2x - 8 \implies x^2 + 5x - 12 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange to standard form.

\textit{Step 3: Solve using the quadratic formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{25 + 48}}{2} = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{73}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = 25 + 48 = 73 \).

\textit{Step 4: Find corresponding \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 4 - 3x = 4 - 3 \times \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{73}}{2} = \frac{23 \mp 3\sqrt{73}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \) into \( y = 4 - 3x \).

\textit{Step 5: Part b: geometric interpretation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{Two points of intersection} \Rightarrow \text{line is a secant to the parabola}
\end{gathered}\]
The line cuts the parabola at two distinct points.

\textit{Step 6: Part c: find the chord length.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta x = \sqrt{73}, \quad \Delta y = -3 \times \sqrt{73} / 1 = -3\sqrt{73}/1
\end{gathered}\]
The difference in \( x \) between the two roots is \( \sqrt{73} \); difference in \( y = -3 \Delta x \).

\textit{Step 7: Apply the distance formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
d = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2} = \sqrt{73 + 9 \times 73} = \sqrt{10 \times 73} = \sqrt{730}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta y = -3\Delta x \) so \( (\Delta y)^2 = 9 \times 73 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad a)  x = $\dfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{73}}{2}$  with corresponding  y  values   b) Secant line to the parabola   c) Chord length  = $\sqrt{730}$ 
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 35\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-035)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 35 (ise2-035)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 10}

\question{A circle has equation \( x^2 + y^2 = 50 \). A line has equation \( y = x + 2 \). \\[3pt] a) Find the coordinates of the two points where the line meets the circle. \\[3pt] b) Find the midpoint of the chord joining these two points. \\[3pt] c) Show that the radius to the midpoint is perpendicular to the chord.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Part a: substitute \( y = x + 2 \) into the circle equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + (x+2)^2 = 50 \implies x^2 + x^2 + 4x + 4 = 50 \implies 2x^2 + 4x - 46 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Substituting the line into the circle reduces both variables to one --- every intersection point must satisfy this single quadratic in \( x \).

\textit{Step 2: Divide through by 2 to simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 2x - 23 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Dividing every term by 2 keeps the equation equivalent. The constant \(-23\) is not a product of integer factors summing to \(2\), so use the quadratic formula.

\textit{Step 3: Apply the quadratic formula with \( a = 1,\ b = 2,\ c = -23 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 92}}{2} = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{96}}{2} = -1 \pm 2\sqrt{6}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = b^2 - 4ac = 4 + 92 = 96 \). Simplify \( \sqrt{96} = \sqrt{16 \cdot 6} = 4\sqrt{6} \), then divide by 2.

\textit{Step 4: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values from \( y = x + 2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = -1 + 2\sqrt{6} \Rightarrow y = 1 + 2\sqrt{6};\quad x = -1 - 2\sqrt{6} \Rightarrow y = 1 - 2\sqrt{6}
\end{gathered}\]
Adding 2 to each \( x \)-value gives the matching \( y \)-value on the line.

\textit{Step 5: Part b: find the midpoint of the chord.}
\[\begin{gathered}
M = \left(\dfrac{(-1+2\sqrt{6})+(-1-2\sqrt{6})}{2},\ \dfrac{(1+2\sqrt{6})+(1-2\sqrt{6})}{2}\right) = (-1,\ 1)
\end{gathered}\]
Average the \( x \)- and \( y \)-coordinates of the endpoints. The \( \pm 2\sqrt{6} \) terms cancel exactly, leaving rational coordinates.

\textit{Step 6: Part c: find the gradient of the chord.}
\[\begin{gathered}
m_{\text{chord}} = 1 \quad (\text{slope of } y = x+2)
\end{gathered}\]
The chord lies along the line \( y = x + 2 \), whose gradient is the coefficient of \( x \), namely 1.

\textit{Step 7: Find the gradient of the radius from the origin to \( M(-1,\ 1) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
m_{\text{radius}} = \dfrac{1 - 0}{-1 - 0} = -1
\end{gathered}\]
The circle \( x^2 + y^2 = 50 \) is centred at the origin, so the radius to \( M \) goes from \( (0,0) \) to \( (-1, 1) \). Apply the gradient formula \( \tfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \).

\textit{Step 8: Check perpendicularity.}
\[\begin{gathered}
m_{\text{chord}} \times m_{\text{radius}} = 1 \times (-1) = -1 \checkmark
\end{gathered}\]
Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular iff the product of their gradients is \( -1 \). This confirms that the radius bisecting a chord is perpendicular to that chord --- a key circle theorem. \( \square \)

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad a)  (-1+2$\sqrt{6}$,  1+2$\sqrt{6}$)  and  (-1-2$\sqrt{6}$,  1-2$\sqrt{6}$)    b) Midpoint  (-1, 1)    c) Gradients multiply to -1, so radius  $\perp$  chord.  $\square$ 
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 36\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-036)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 36 (ise2-036)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 2x + y = 7 \) and \( x - y = 2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Add the equations to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x + y) + (x - y) = 7 + 2 \implies 3x = 9 \implies x = 3
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients are \( +1 \) and \( -1 \), so adding eliminates \( y \) immediately --- no scaling needed.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( x = 3 \) into the first equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2(3) + y = 7 \implies y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Back-substitute into either original equation. Quick check in the second: \( 3 - 1 = 2 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 3, y = 1\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 37\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-037)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 37 (ise2-037)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 3x + 2y = 12 \) and \( x + 2y = 8 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(3x + 2y) - (x + 2y) = 12 - 8 \implies 2x = 4 \implies x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients match (\( +2 \) in both), so subtracting cancels \( y \). Be careful with signs on the right-hand side: \( 12 - 8 = 4 \), not \( 12 + 8 \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( x = 2 \) into the second equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 + 2y = 8 \implies 2y = 6 \implies y = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Choose the simpler equation for back-substitution. Verify in the first: \( 6 + 6 = 12 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 2, y = 3\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 38\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-038)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 38 (ise2-038)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 4x - 3y = 5 \) and \( 2x + 3y = 13 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Add the equations to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(4x - 3y) + (2x + 3y) = 5 + 13 \implies 6x = 18 \implies x = 3
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients are \( -3 \) and \( +3 \) --- opposite, so adding cancels them straight away.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( x = 3 \) into the second equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2(3) + 3y = 13 \implies 3y = 7 \implies y = \tfrac{7}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
A non-integer answer is perfectly valid. Quick check in the first equation: \( 12 - 7 = 5 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 3, y = \frac{7}{3}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 39\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-039)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 39 (ise2-039)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 5x + 4y = 22 \) and \( 3x - 4y = 2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Add the equations to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(5x + 4y) + (3x - 4y) = 22 + 2 \implies 8x = 24 \implies x = 3
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-coefficients are \( +4 \) and \( -4 \), so adding the equations cancels \( y \) without any scaling.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( x = 3 \) into the first equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
5(3) + 4y = 22 \implies 4y = 7 \implies y = \tfrac{7}{4}
\end{gathered}\]
A non-integer answer is fine. Quick check in the second: \( 9 - 7 = 2 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 3, y = \frac{7}{4}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 40\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-040)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 40 (ise2-040)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( x + 3y = 10 \) and \( 2x - y = 6 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the second equation, rearrange for \( y \) and substitute into the first.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2x - 6 \implies x + 3(2x - 6) = 10 \implies 7x = 28 \implies x = 4
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \) in equation 2 has coefficient \( -1 \), so substitution is the cleanest route. Distribute the 3 carefully across both terms: \( 3(2x - 6) = 6x - 18 \).

\textit{Step 2: Find \( y \) using \( y = 2x - 6 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2(4) - 6 = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Back-substitute into the rearranged equation. Verify in the first: \( 4 + 6 = 10 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 4, y = 2\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 41\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-041)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 41 (ise2-041)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( \frac{x}{2} + y = 5 \) and \( x - 2y = 4 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Multiply the first equation by 2 to clear the fraction.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times \left(\tfrac{x}{2} + y\right) = 2 \times 5 \implies x + 2y = 10
\end{gathered}\]
Clearing fractions before eliminating is almost always cleaner than working with fractions throughout. Multiplying every term by 2 preserves equality.

\textit{Step 2: Add the new first equation to the second to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x + 2y) + (x - 2y) = 10 + 4 \implies 2x = 14 \implies x = 7,\; y = \tfrac{3}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( y \)-terms cancel. Back-substitute into \( x + 2y = 10 \): \( 2y = 3 \), so \( y = \tfrac{3}{2} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 7, y = \frac{3}{2}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 42\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-042)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 42 (ise2-042)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Two numbers add to 20 and differ by 6. Find the numbers.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Translate the words into two linear equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x + y = 20; \quad x - y = 6
\end{gathered}\]
"Add to 20" gives the sum; "differ by 6" gives the difference (taking the larger minus the smaller).

\textit{Step 2: Add the equations to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x + y) + (x - y) = 20 + 6 \implies 2x = 26 \implies x = 13,\; y = 7
\end{gathered}\]
Adding cancels \( y \) directly. Back-substitute \( x = 13 \) into \( x + y = 20 \) to get \( y = 7 \). Check: \( 13 - 7 = 6 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle 13 \) and \(\displaystyle  7\)
\end{answerbox}

\question{Solve: \( 3x + 5y = 21 \) and \( 2x + 3y = 13 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Scale to align \( y \)-coefficients: multiply eq1 by 3 and eq2 by 5.}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(3x + 5y) = 63 \implies 9x + 15y = 63; \quad 5(2x + 3y) = 65 \implies 10x + 15y = 65
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply each whole equation by an integer to make the \( y \)-coefficients both equal 15. Scaling preserves the solution set of each equation.

\textit{Step 2: Subtract to eliminate \( y \), then back-substitute.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(10x + 15y) - (9x + 15y) = 65 - 63 \implies x = 2,\; y = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Watch signs carefully when subtracting. Back-substituting \( x = 2 \) into \( 2x + 3y = 13 \) gives \( 3y = 9 \), so \( y = 3 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 2, y = 3\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 44\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-044)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 44 (ise2-044)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{A cinema sells adult tickets at \( \pounds 8 \) and child tickets at \( \pounds 5 \). 50 tickets are sold for \( \pounds 310 \). How many of each?}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Define variables and write two equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
a + c = 50; \quad 8a + 5c = 310
\end{gathered}\]
Let \( a \) be the number of adult tickets and \( c \) the number of child tickets. The total count gives one equation; the total revenue gives the other.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( c = 50 - a \) into the revenue equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
8a + 5(50 - a) = 310 \implies 8a + 250 - 5a = 310 \implies 3a = 60 \implies a = 20
\end{gathered}\]
Substitution is cleanest because \( a + c = 50 \) has unit coefficients. Distribute the 5 and collect like terms.

\textit{Step 3: Find \( c \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
c = 50 - 20 = 30
\end{gathered}\]
Verify the revenue: \( 8 \times 20 + 5 \times 30 = 160 + 150 = 310 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad 20 adult, 30 child
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 45\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-045)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 45 (ise2-045)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( y = x^2 \) and \( y = 2x + 3 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the two expressions for \( y \) equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 = 2x + 3 \implies x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
At any intersection both equations give the same \( y \). Move all terms to one side to form a quadratic in \( x \).

\textit{Step 2: Factorise the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = 3 \text{ or } x = -1
\end{gathered}\]
Find two numbers multiplying to \( -3 \) and summing to \( -2 \): they are \( -3 \) and \( +1 \).

\textit{Step 3: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 3:\; y = 9; \quad x = -1:\; y = 1
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into \( y = x^2 \) (or equivalently the line). Both endpoints must satisfy both equations.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (3, 9) \) and \(\displaystyle  (-1, 1)\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 46\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-046)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 46 (ise2-046)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( y = x^2 - 4 \) and \( y = 3x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the two expressions for \( y \) equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 - 4 = 3x \implies x^2 - 3x - 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Both equations give the same \( y \) at any intersection, so equate them. Move everything to one side to form a quadratic.

\textit{Step 2: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 4)(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = 4 \text{ or } x = -1
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to \( -4 \) and summing to \( -3 \) are \( -4 \) and \( +1 \).

\textit{Step 3: Find the matching \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 4:\; y = 12; \quad x = -1:\; y = -3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into \( y = 3x \) (the simpler equation). Check in the curve: \( 16 - 4 = 12 \) and \( 1 - 4 = -3 \) \(\checkmark\).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (4, 12) \) and \(\displaystyle  (-1, -3)\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 47\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-047)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 47 (ise2-047)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Solve: \( x + y = 5 \) and \( x^2 + y^2 = 13 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the linear equation, express \( y \) in terms of \( x \) and substitute.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 5 - x \implies x^2 + (5 - x)^2 = 13
\end{gathered}\]
Substituting from the linear equation reduces the circle equation to a single-variable quadratic.

\textit{Step 2: Expand and simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 25 - 10x + x^2 = 13 \implies 2x^2 - 10x + 12 = 0 \implies x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand \( (5 - x)^2 = 25 - 10x + x^2 \), then divide through by 2 to keep coefficients small.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise and pair with the matching \( y \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 \implies x = 2, y = 3 \text{ or } x = 3, y = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 6 and summing to \( -5 \) are \( -2 \) and \( -3 \). Use \( y = 5 - x \) to find the matching \( y \)-coordinate.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (2, 3) \) and \(\displaystyle  (3, 2)\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 48\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-048)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 48 (ise2-048)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 2x - 3y = 1 \) and \( 4x + y = 15 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the second equation, rearrange \( y = 15 - 4x \) and substitute.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x - 3(15 - 4x) = 1 \implies 2x - 45 + 12x = 1 \implies 14x = 46 \implies x = \tfrac{23}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
The second equation has \( y \) with coefficient \( +1 \), so substitution is cleanest. Distribute the \( -3 \) carefully --- sign errors here are common.

\textit{Step 2: Find \( y \) using \( y = 15 - 4x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 15 - 4 \times \tfrac{23}{7} = \tfrac{105 - 92}{7} = \tfrac{13}{7}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert 15 to \( \tfrac{105}{7} \) before subtracting. Always back-substitute into the rearranged equation.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = \frac{23}{7}, y = \frac{13}{7}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 49\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-049)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 49 (ise2-049)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( y = x^2 + 1 \) and \( y = 5 - x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the two expressions for \( y \) equal.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 1 = 5 - x \implies x^2 + x - 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Equating the two expressions for \( y \) gives a quadratic in \( x \) whose roots are the \( x \)-coordinates of the intersection points.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the quadratic formula since the quadratic does not factorise over the integers.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 16}}{2} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = b^2 - 4ac = 1 + 16 = 17 \), not a perfect square, so the solutions are irrational.

\textit{Step 3: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values from \( y = 5 - x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 5 - \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} = \dfrac{11 \mp \sqrt{17}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Write 5 with a denominator of 2 and combine. The \( \mp \) symbol mirrors the original \( \pm \) because we subtract.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}, \; y = \frac{11 \mp \sqrt{17}}{2}\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 50\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-050)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 50 (ise2-050)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The sum of two numbers is 15 and their product is 54. Find the two numbers.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Translate the words into equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x + y = 15; \quad xy = 54
\end{gathered}\]
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be the two numbers. "Sum" gives a linear equation; "product" gives a quadratic relation.

\textit{Step 2: From the linear equation, substitute \( y = 15 - x \) into the product equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x(15 - x) = 54 \implies 15x - x^2 = 54 \implies x^2 - 15x + 54 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Expand and rearrange to a quadratic in \( x \). The two roots will be the two numbers themselves.

\textit{Step 3: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x - 6)(x - 9) = 0 \implies x = 6 \text{ or } x = 9
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 54 and summing to \( -15 \) are \( -6 \) and \( -9 \). The two solutions just swap which number is "\( x \)" and which is "\( y \)".

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle 6 \) and \(\displaystyle  9\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 51\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-051)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 51 (ise2-051)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Solve: \( 3x - 2y = 4 \) and \( 6x - 4y = 8 \). What do you notice?}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Compare the two equations: equation 2 is exactly equation 1 multiplied by 2.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times (3x - 2y) = 2 \times 4 \implies 6x - 4y = 8 \quad \text{(identical to eq2)}
\end{gathered}\]
When one equation is a non-zero scalar multiple of the other, the two equations describe the SAME line. Every point on that line satisfies both.

\textit{Step 2: State the conclusion.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\text{Infinitely many solutions: any } (x, y) \text{ on } y = \tfrac{3x - 4}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
There is no unique solution because the system is dependent --- geometrically, the two lines coincide.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Infinitely many solutions (the two equations describe the same line)
\end{answerbox}

\small The two equations plotted, with the solution shown at the point(s) of intersection.\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 52\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-052)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 52 (ise2-052)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Solve: \( 2x + 3y = 7 \) and \( 4x + 6y = 10 \). What do you notice?}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Multiply the first equation by 2 and compare with the second.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 \times (2x + 3y) = 14 \implies 4x + 6y = 14, \text{ but eq2 says } 4x + 6y = 10
\end{gathered}\]
The left-hand sides match exactly but the right-hand sides do not. This is a contradiction --- no \( (x, y) \) can satisfy both equations simultaneously.

\textit{Step 2: Interpret geometrically.}
\[\begin{gathered}
14 \neq 10 \implies \text{lines are parallel and distinct}
\end{gathered}\]
The two lines have the same gradient (same ratio of coefficients) but different intercepts, so they never meet.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad No solution (the lines are parallel and distinct)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 53\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-053)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 53 (ise2-053)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( y = 2x^2 - 3 \) and \( y = 5x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the two expressions for \( y \) equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x^2 - 3 = 5x \implies 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Equating the two expressions for \( y \) gives a quadratic in \( x \) whose roots are the \( x \)-coordinates of the intersection points.

\textit{Step 2: Factorise.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0 \implies x = -\tfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } x = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Use the AC method: find factors of \( 2 \times (-3) = -6 \) that sum to \( -5 \), namely \( -6 \) and \( +1 \). Splitting \( -5x \) and grouping gives the bracketed factorisation.

\textit{Step 3: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values from \( y = 5x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = -\tfrac{1}{2}:\; y = -\tfrac{5}{2}; \quad x = 3:\; y = 15
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into the simpler equation. Check in the curve: \( 2(9) - 3 = 15 \checkmark \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (-\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{5}{2}) \) and \(\displaystyle  (3, 15)\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 54\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-054)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 54 (ise2-054)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Find the value(s) of \( k \) such that \( y = kx - 3 \) is tangent to \( y = x^2 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the expressions for \( y \) equal and rearrange to a quadratic in \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 = kx - 3 \implies x^2 - kx + 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
At any intersection point, both equations give the same \( y \). Bringing all terms to one side gives a quadratic whose roots are the \( x \)-coordinates of the intersections.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the tangency condition: the discriminant must equal zero.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = (-k)^2 - 4(1)(3) = k^2 - 12 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
A tangent line meets the curve at exactly one point, which corresponds to a repeated root of the quadratic --- equivalently \( \Delta = 0 \).

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( k \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
k^2 = 12 \implies k = \pm 2\sqrt{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Take square roots, remembering both signs. \( \sqrt{12} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 3} = 2\sqrt{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle k = \pm 2\sqrt{3}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 55\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-055)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 55 (ise2-055)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( x + 2y = 8 \) and \( xy = 6 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the linear equation, express \( x = 8 - 2y \) and substitute into the product equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(8 - 2y)y = 6 \implies 8y - 2y^2 = 6 \implies 2y^2 - 8y + 6 = 0 \implies y^2 - 4y + 3 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Substitution turns a linear-plus-product system into a single quadratic in \( y \). Divide by 2 to keep coefficients small.

\textit{Step 2: Factorise and pair with the matching \( x \)-values.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(y - 1)(y - 3) = 0 \implies y = 1,\ x = 6 \text{ or } y = 3,\ x = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Numbers multiplying to 3 and summing to \( -4 \) are \( -1 \) and \( -3 \). Use \( x = 8 - 2y \) for the matching \( x \)-coordinate.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (6, 1) \) and \(\displaystyle  (2, 3)\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 56\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-056)}}

\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 7x + 2y = 20 \) and \( 3x + 5y = 21 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Scale to align \( y \)-coefficients: multiply eq1 by 5 and eq2 by 2.}
\[\begin{gathered}
5(7x + 2y) = 100 \implies 35x + 10y = 100; \quad 2(3x + 5y) = 42 \implies 6x + 10y = 42
\end{gathered}\]
Multiplying both equations preserves their solutions and produces a common \( y \)-coefficient of 10. Subtracting will then eliminate \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Subtract to eliminate \( y \) and back-substitute.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(35x + 10y) - (6x + 10y) = 100 - 42 \implies 29x = 58 \implies x = 2,\; y = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Sign-track carefully: \( 35x - 6x = 29x \) and \( 100 - 42 = 58 \). Back-substitute \( x = 2 \) into \( 7x + 2y = 20 \): \( 2y = 6 \), so \( y = 3 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = 2, y = 3\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 57\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-057)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 57 (ise2-057)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{A rectangle has perimeter 28 cm. Its length is 4 cm more than its width. Find the dimensions.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Translate the words into two equations.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2l + 2w = 28; \quad l = w + 4
\end{gathered}\]
Perimeter \( = 2(l + w) \); "4 cm more than width" gives \( l = w + 4 \). Two equations in two unknowns.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( l = w + 4 \) into the perimeter equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2(w + 4) + 2w = 28 \implies 4w + 8 = 28 \implies 4w = 20 \implies w = 5,\; l = 9
\end{gathered}\]
Substitution is cleanest here because one equation already isolates \( l \). Distribute the 2, collect terms, then back-substitute for \( l \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad Width 5 cm, length 9 cm
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 58\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-058)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 58 (ise2-058)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( y = x^2 - 2x \) and \( y + x = 4 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: From the linear equation, \( y = 4 - x \). Substitute into the quadratic.}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 - x = x^2 - 2x \implies x^2 - x - 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange the linear equation first so that the substitution into the quadratic only involves one variable.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the quadratic formula.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 16}}{2} = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \Delta = 1 + 16 = 17 \), not a perfect square, so the answer is irrational. Both roots correspond to real intersection points.

\textit{Step 3: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values from \( y = 4 - x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 4 - \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} = \dfrac{7 \mp \sqrt{17}}{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Express 4 with denominator 2 (\( 4 = \tfrac{8}{2} \)) and combine. The sign flips because we subtract.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}, \; y = \frac{7 \mp \sqrt{17}}{2}\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 59\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-059)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 59 (ise2-059)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Solve: \( \frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{4} = 1 \) and \( \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{3} = 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Clear fractions by multiplying each equation by its LCM of denominators.}
\[\begin{gathered}
12 \times (\tfrac{x}{3} + \tfrac{y}{4}) = 12 \implies 4x + 3y = 12;\quad 6 \times (\tfrac{x}{2} - \tfrac{y}{3}) = 6 \implies 3x - 2y = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Always clear fractions before eliminating --- keeps the arithmetic clean and avoids stray denominators.

\textit{Step 2: Scale to align \( y \)-coefficients and add to eliminate \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
2(4x + 3y) + 3(3x - 2y) = 24 + 18 \implies 8x + 6y + 9x - 6y = 42 \implies 17x = 42 \implies x = \tfrac{42}{17}
\end{gathered}\]
Multiplying eq1 by 2 and eq2 by 3 makes the \( y \)-coefficients \( +6 \) and \( -6 \). Adding cancels \( y \).

\textit{Step 3: Back-substitute into \( 4x + 3y = 12 \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3y = 12 - 4 \times \tfrac{42}{17} = \tfrac{204 - 168}{17} = \tfrac{36}{17} \implies y = \tfrac{12}{17}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert 12 to \( \tfrac{204}{17} \) before subtracting. Then divide by 3.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = \frac{42}{17}, y = \frac{12}{17}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 60\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-060)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 60 (ise2-060)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find the coordinates where \( y = x^2 + 2x - 5 \) meets \( y = 2x + 3 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the two expressions for \( y \) equal and simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 2x - 5 = 2x + 3 \implies x^2 = 8 \implies x = \pm 2\sqrt{2}
\end{gathered}\]
The \( 2x \) terms cancel on each side, leaving \( x^2 = 8 \). Take both square roots: \( \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Find the corresponding \( y \)-values from \( y = 2x + 3 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x = 2\sqrt{2}:\; y = 4\sqrt{2} + 3; \quad x = -2\sqrt{2}:\; y = 3 - 4\sqrt{2}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute each \( x \)-value into the linear equation. The two intersection points are symmetric about the \( y \)-axis offset by the line's slope.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle (2\sqrt{2}, 4\sqrt{2}+3) \) and \(\displaystyle  (-2\sqrt{2}, 3-4\sqrt{2})\)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 61\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-061)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 61 (ise2-061)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Solve: \( 5x - 2y = 11 \) and \( 3x + 4y = 1 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Multiply eq1 by 2 to align \( y \)-coefficients, then add to eq2.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2(5x - 2y) = 22 \implies 10x - 4y = 22; \quad (10x - 4y) + (3x + 4y) = 22 + 1 \implies 13x = 23 \implies x = \tfrac{23}{13}
\end{gathered}\]
Doubling eq1 makes the \( y \)-coefficients \( -4 \) and \( +4 \), so adding eliminates \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Back-substitute into \( 3x + 4y = 1 \) to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4y = 1 - 3 \times \tfrac{23}{13} = \tfrac{13 - 69}{13} = -\tfrac{56}{13} \implies y = -\tfrac{14}{13}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert 1 to \( \tfrac{13}{13} \) before subtracting. Divide by 4 to isolate \( y \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle x = \frac{23}{13}, y = -\frac{14}{13}\)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Simultaneous Equations 62\quad\small\texttt{(ise2-062)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Simultaneous Equations 62 (ise2-062)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The line \( y = mx + 1 \) is tangent to \( y = x^2 + 2 \). Find the possible values of \( m \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Set the expressions for \( y \) equal and rearrange.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2 + 2 = mx + 1 \implies x^2 - mx + 1 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
At any intersection both expressions for \( y \) must agree. Collecting on one side gives a quadratic whose roots are the \( x \)-coordinates of the intersection points.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the tangency condition: discriminant equals zero.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\Delta = (-m)^2 - 4(1)(1) = m^2 - 4 = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Tangency means exactly one solution, so the quadratic has a repeated root --- equivalently \( \Delta = 0 \).

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( m \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
m^2 = 4 \implies m = \pm 2
\end{gathered}\]
Take both square roots. The two values correspond to the two distinct tangent lines passing through \( (0,\ 1) \) and touching the parabola.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle m = \pm 2\)
\end{answerbox}
